name: Forgiveness
text: Forgiving those who wrong us, pardon of sins, letting go of resentment and revenge, being forgiven.

Mencius said, "Benevolence overcomes what is not benevolent as water overcomes fire. Those who practice benevolence today are like someone trying to put out a cartload of burning firewood with a single cup of water; when the fire is not put out, they say that water cannot overcome fire. This goes far toward siding with what is most unbenevolent, and in the end they are sure to lose even what little they have."

Mencius said, "Benevolence is the human heart; righteousness is the human road. How sad it is when people abandon their road and do not follow it, and let go of their heart and do not know how to seek it! When people's chickens and dogs stray, they know to go after them; but when their heart strays, they do not know to go after it. The way of learning is nothing else than seeking the strayed heart."

The doctrine of Redemption is the fundamental mystery of our holy religion, and whoso believeth in it shall not perish, but have everlasting life in which to try to understand it.

557. attricioun, attrition. 'An imperfect sorrow for sin, as if a bruising which does not amount to utter crushing (contrition); horror of sin through fear of punishment ... while contrition has its motive in the love of God;' New E. Dict.

GLOSE. As thus: that, yif a wight have prosperitee, he is a good man and worthy to han that prosperitee; and who-so hath adversitee, he is a wikked man, and god hath forsake him, and he is worthy to han that adversitee. This is the opinioun of some 210 folk.

392. Scathe. Harm, mischief. Spenser uses the word often; as in F. Q. i. 12, 34: "To worke new woe and improvided scath," etc. Cf. Shakespeare, K. John, ii. 1. 75: "To do offence and scathe in Christendom;" Rich. III. i. 3. 317: "To pray for them that have done scathe to us," etc.

170. Reave. Tear away. The participle reft is still used, at least in poetry. Cf. Shakespeare, V. and A. 766: "Or butcher-sire that reaves his son of life" (that is, bereaves); Spenser, F. Q. i. 3. 36: "He to him lept, in minde to reave his life;" Id. ii. 8. 15: "I will him reave of arms," etc.

“Forgive I cannot, and do not wish to, and I regard it as wrong. I have done everything for this woman, and she has trodden it all in the mud to which she is akin. I am not a spiteful man, I have never hated anyone, but I hate her with my whole soul, and I cannot even forgive her, because I hate her too much for all the wrong she has done me!” he said, with tones of hatred in his voice.
